subject: physiology
title: Hearing and vestibular function: high-yield physiology

steps.tx: The **organ of Corti** sits on the basilar membrane inside the scala media and holds the auditory receptors. Its hair cells are arranged in one row of inner hair cells and three to four rows of outer hair cells. Each hair cell's stereocilia are embedded in the tectorial membrane. The scala media is filled with **endolymph**, a potassium-rich fluid that is electrically positive, at about +85 mV, because the stria vascularis secretes potassium into it.
steps.say: The organ of Corti sits on the basilar membrane inside the scala media and holds the auditory receptors. Its hair cells form one row of inner hair cells and three to four rows of outer hair cells. The stereocilia are embedded in the tectorial membrane. The scala media is filled with endolymph, a potassium-rich fluid that is electrically positive, at about plus 85 millivolts, because the stria vascularis secretes potassium into it.

steps.tx: Sound moves the basilar membrane, creating a shearing force between the reticular lamina and the tectorial membrane. The stereocilia bend and open **potassium channels**, so potassium enters and depolarises the hair cell. Voltage-gated calcium channels then open, calcium enters, and **glutamate** is released onto the eighth nerve. Inner hair cells supply about 90 to 95 percent of the afferent fibres.

steps.tx: Frequency is coded by **place theory**. A travelling wave builds up along the basilar membrane and peaks at the point whose resonant frequency matches the sound. High-frequency sounds peak near the base by the oval window, while low frequencies travel to the apex near the helicotrema. The auditory pathway runs from the spiral ganglion to the cochlear nuclei, superior olivary complex, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate body and auditory cortex, Brodmann area 41.

steps.tx: The middle ear ossicles act as a **lever** that transfers energy from the large tympanic membrane to the small oval window, raising efficiency of transmission. Interference by the stapedius and tensor tympani muscles reduces this transfer. The Eustachian tube is separate and does not depend on the ossicles. Intensity of sound is measured in decibels.

vis.alt: Impedance matching of the middle ear: the large tympanic membrane area focuses force on the small oval window, about a 17 fold area gain, the ossicular lever adds about 1.3, giving roughly 22 fold pressure gain that overcomes air to fluid reflection of sound.
vis.caption: Area ratio times lever ratio gives about 22 times pressure gain; without it most sound would reflect from the cochlear fluid.

steps.tx: The **otolith organs**, the utricle and saccule, detect linear acceleration, gravity and head tilt. Their macula contains hair cells beneath a membrane of calcium carbonate otoconia. The three **semicircular canals** sense angular acceleration. Each canal ends in an ampulla whose crista holds hair cells under a cupula. Endolymph inertia bends the cupula during rotation, and the canals sit at right angles to one another.

steps.tx: The image shows the inner ear beside a magnified macula with **otolith organs** holding crystals called otoconia over hair cells. Tilt or forward motion shifts this weighted membrane and bends the hairs, signalling position to the brain. The three **semicircular canals** nearby sense rotation instead. This split explains why one system reports gravity while the other reports turning during everyday movement.
steps.say: This panel pairs the whole inner ear with a close view of the macula, where otoconia crystals rest on a membrane above hair cells. When the head tilts or the body moves in a straight line, the heavy crystal layer lags and bends the hairs, which reports gravity and linear motion. The looped canals handle turning separately. Remember macula for tilt and straight line movement, canals for rotation.
